sources.title: Direct effects of illustrative tax changes bulletin (June 2025)
sources.notes: Methodology notes: direct effects on the tax base and closely related bases; behavioural responses via taxable income elasticities and tax-motivated incorporation; wider economic effects excluded; rate changes scale roughly linearly, allowances and limits do not; CGT and SDLT non-linear and asymmetrical.

sources.title: Statement of Funding Policy: Funding the Scottish Government, Welsh Government and Northern Ireland Executive
sources.notes: Barnett formula (paragraphs 3.9-3.18): change to planned UK Government departmental spending × comparability factor × population proportion, applied to resource and capital DEL separately. Annex B lists the departmental comparability factors used at Spending Review 2025; the FCDO and Ministry of Defence undertake only reserved activities and have none (B.12).

sources.title: Estimated cost of tax reliefs
sources.notes: Table 2 gives six-year cost estimates (£ million, 2020-21 to 2025-26) of each tax relief; the later years are projections. They are estimates of the cost of the relief as it stands, not forecasts of what removing it would raise; see the background quality report.

sources.title: Background quality report: tax relief statistics
sources.notes: Section 4, Accuracy and reliability: "These figures should be interpreted as estimates of the amount of relief which is claimed and subsequently granted each year. These estimates do not represent the gain to the exchequer should a relief be abolished." Costs are on an accruals basis.

sources.title: Autumn Budget 2024 Table 5.1: policy decisions
sources.notes: Certified costings of Autumn Budget 2024 measures, £ million 2024-25 to 2029-30, positive reduces borrowing. Lines used: 25 (additional-dwellings stamp duty surcharge 3% to 5%), 27 (capital gains tax main rates to 18% and 24% with BADR and IR changes), 30 (inheritance tax thresholds frozen to April 2030).

sources.title: Forecasts for the UK economy: a comparison of independent forecasts
sources.notes: Averages of independent forecasts. Short term: 2026 GDP growth 1.1%, CPI Q4 3.3%, RPI Q4 4.2%, PSNB 2026-27 £119.0bn; 2027 GDP 1.1%, CPI 2.3%. Medium term (calendar years 2026 to 2030): GDP 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.4, 1.5%; CPI 3.1, 2.7, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0%; RPI 3.7, 3.8, 3.2, 2.9, 2.8%; PSNB (2026-27 to 2030-31) £126.4bn, 106.6, 99.5, 90.3, 82.2. HMT states that the averages and ranges may be reproduced free of charge provided they are reproduced accurately and not used in a misleading context; the underlying forecasts remain the copyright of the forecasting organisations.

sources.title: Finance Act 2007, section 1: charge and rates for 2007-08
sources.notes: For 2007-08 the starting rate was 10%, the basic rate 22% and the higher rate 40%.

sources.title: Finance Act 2008, section 1: charge and main rates for 2008-09
sources.notes: For 2008-09 the basic rate is 20% and the higher rate 40%; the basic rate has been 20% since.

sources.title: Finance Act 2012, section 1: charge for 2012-13 and rates for 2012-13 and subsequent tax years
sources.notes: Additional rate 50% for 2012-13 and 45% from 2013-14; basic rate 20%, higher rate 40%.

sources.title: Finance Act 2021, section 5: basic rate limit and personal allowance for future tax years (as amended)
sources.notes: Sets the basic rate limit at £37,700 and the personal allowance at £12,570 for 2022-23 to 2030-31 (the later years added by amendment), switching off indexation for those years.

sources.title: Rates and allowances for Income Tax: current and past
sources.notes: Personal allowance £12,570 and basic rate limit £37,700 in each year 2023-24 to 2026-27; basic rate 20%, higher rate 40% (£37,701 to £125,140 of taxable income), additional rate 45%.

sources.title: Rates and allowances: National Insurance contributions
sources.notes: 2026-27: employee (Class 1) 8% between the primary threshold (£242 a week) and the upper earnings limit (£967), 2% above; employer 15% above the secondary threshold (£96 a week), 13.8% up to 2024-25; Class 4 self-employed 6% between £12,570 and £50,270 and 2% above.

sources.title: Rates and allowances: Corporation Tax
sources.notes: Main rate 25% for profits over £250,000 from April 2023 (19% in 2022); small profits rate 19%; marginal relief between £50,000 and £250,000.

sources.title: Inheritance Tax thresholds and interest rates
sources.notes: Nil-rate band £325,000 from 6 April 2009 to 5 April 2031; £312,000 in 2008-09.

sources.title: Excise Duty hydrocarbon oils rates
sources.notes: Unleaded petrol and diesel 52.95p per litre from 23 March 2022.

sources.title: Capital Gains Tax: rates
sources.notes: Higher and additional rate taxpayers pay 24% on gains from 6 April 2026; basic rate taxpayers pay 18% on gains within their remaining basic rate band and 24% above it.

sources.title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: residential property rates
sources.notes: Single property: 0% to £125,000, 2% to £250,000, 5% to £925,000, 10% to £1.5 million, 12% above; usually 5% on top if you own another residential property.

sources.title: VAT rates
sources.notes: Standard rate 20% since 4 January 2011 (17.5% before); reduced rate 5% (for example children's car seats and home energy); zero rate (for example most food and children's clothes); some things exempt (postage stamps, financial and property transactions).

sources.title: VAT rates on different goods and services
sources.notes: Lists the goods and services at 0%, 5% and 20%: most food and drink, children's clothes and footwear, books and newspapers, passenger transport for 10 or more, construction of new dwellings at 0%; domestic fuel and power at 5%.

sources.title: Alcohol Duty rates
sources.notes: Rates from 1 February 2026 per litre of pure alcohol: beer 1.3% to 3.4% ABV £9.96, 3.5% to 8.4% £22.58, 8.5% to 22% £30.62, above 22% £33.99; still cider 3.5% to 8.4% £10.39.

sources.title: Child Benefit: what you'll get
sources.notes: Weekly rates: £27.05 for the eldest or only child, £17.90 for each additional child.

sources.title: Bank of England Interactive Statistical Database: 10-year nominal par gilt yield (IUDMNZC)
sources.notes: Daily series. 4.63% on 2 January 2026; 5.35% on 11 September 2026 (with Bank Rate 3.75%).

sources.title: RPI all items, percentage change over 12 months (CZBH, MM23)

sources.title: How Inheritance Tax works: thresholds, rules and allowances
sources.notes: The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%, charged on the part of the estate above the threshold.

sources.title: Public Expenditure Statistical Analyses 2025, chapter 4 tables
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. Table 4.3 gives public sector expenditure on services by function in real terms (£ billion, 2024-25 prices) and Table 4.4 the same as a share of GDP, both 2002-03 to 2024-25. Function spending covers the whole public sector, including local government and the devolved administrations, so it is wider than a UK Government department's budget.

sources.title: Benefit expenditure and caseload tables 2026: outturn and forecast tables
sources.notes: Official statistics in development. Table 1a gives expenditure by benefit in nominal terms, 1948-49 to 2030-31, on the same forecast as the OBR’s. The State Pension line is the base for costing a change to how the pension is uprated.

sources.title: International Development (Official Development Assistance Target) Act 2015
sources.notes: Section 1 puts a duty on the Secretary of State to meet the 0.7 per cent of gross national income target for official development assistance. Section 2 covers the accountability to Parliament if the target is not met in a year.

sources.title: Schools, pupils and their characteristics
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. 8,920,227 pupils in all schools, of which 8,355,420 in state-funded schools. 2,214,994 eligible for free school meals on the benefits criteria (26.5% of state-funded pupils). Almost 1.6 million infants took a free meal on census day, of whom over 1.2 million through universal infant free school meals. The state-funded totals are sums of the published school-type rows; the department prints no single state-funded total.

sources.title: Universal infant free school meals: conditions of grant 2026 to 2027
sources.notes: "A meal rate uplift to £2.66 will be implemented for the 2026 to 2027 academic year... An allocation assumes that pupils will take 190 school meals over an academic year, providing £505 per eligible pupil."

sources.title: Free school meals expansion grant: methodology
sources.notes: From the 2026/27 academic year free school meals in England are extended to every child in a household on universal credit, funded with "over £1 billion over the multi-year spending review period from 2026 to 2029". Confirms the schools national funding formula free school meal factor at £505 a pupil a year.

sources.title: Student loan forecasts for England
sources.notes: Official statistics. Table 1 gives loan outlay by product; Table 4b the Resource Accounting and Budgeting charge; Table 4c the transfer proportion, which is the share of loan outlay that scores as government expenditure in the national accounts.

sources.title: Student loans in the public sector finances: a methodological guide
sources.notes: "Splitting lending into two components: a genuine loan and government spending. This new approach recognises that a significant proportion of student loan debt will never be repaid by recording government expenditure related to the cancellation of student loans in the period that loans are issued." The loaned portion is a financial transaction; only the transfer portion scores in borrowing.

sources.title: Changes to tuition fees: 2026 to 2027 academic year and 2027 to 2028 academic year
sources.notes: The maximum tuition fee for a standard full-time course at a provider with a Teaching Excellence Framework award and an access and participation plan is £9,790 in 2026/27 and £10,050 in 2027/28.

sources.title: Nationalising the water sector: how we assessed the cost
sources.notes: "The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) has estimated that nationalising the water industry would cost approximately £100 billion." The regulatory capital value of the sector was £99.3bn in 2024 and £106.7bn in 2025. Defra treats that value as debt plus equity and applies no discount or premium, on the ground that creditors could demand compensation immediately.

sources.title: Monthly statistics on the public sector finances: a methodological guide
sources.notes: Section 5.1.3: "When cash is used to purchase a financial asset of equal value, there is no change to overall indebtedness... Hence there is no expenditure and the transaction has no impact on PSNB. However, there is necessarily a cash payment, which impacts on PSNCR." Section 5.1.4 adds that reclassifying a body into the public sector changes net debt without any cash moving.

sources.title: Consolidated budgeting guidance 2025-26
sources.notes: Chapter 8: financial transactions "do not score as spending and there is no immediate effect on Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities (PSNFL)... This will increase public sector net debt (PSND)". Purchases of equity score in a ringfence within capital DEL. Chapter 3: capital grants score in the capital budget and affect public sector net investment.

sources.title: Spending Review 2025
sources.notes: Confirms £39bn for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme over ten years from 2026-27, reaching £4bn a year in 2029-30; official development assistance falling to 0.3% of gross national income by 2027; and NATO-qualifying defence spending reaching 2.6% of GDP by 2027.

sources.title: Social and Affordable Homes Programme 2026 to 2036: policy statement
sources.notes: "could deliver around 300,000 affordable homes over its lifetime, with around 180,000 for Social Rent." At least 60% of homes must be for social rent. The department does not publish standard grant rates: "we are not publishing standard grant rates".

sources.title: Affordable housing supply in England: 2024 to 2025
sources.notes: National Statistics. 64,762 affordable homes completed in England in 2024-25, the highest since 2014-15, of which 12,198 for social rent, the highest since 2012-13.

sources.title: A wealth tax for the UK: Wealth Tax Commission final report
sources.notes: Advani, Chamberlain and Summers. Table ES.2 and Table 8: an annual wealth tax above £10m at 1.12% raises £9.9bn with low avoidance and £8.7bn with high avoidance, from 22,000 taxpayers, before administration costs. Section 6.3 warns that its analysis "has been constrained by a lack of reliable data on individuals with total wealth above £10 million".

sources.title: Revenue and distributional modelling for a wealth tax (Evidence Paper 13)
sources.notes: Advani, Hughson and Tarrant. Table 1 gives the annual wealth tax rates and revenues. Section 3.1: behavioural responses to a 1% rate are assumed to cut the tax base by 7% to 17%, the low and high avoidance scenarios. A 10% non-compliance rate is applied separately.

sources.title: Household total wealth in Great Britain: April 2020 to March 2022
sources.notes: The wealthiest 1% of households hold at least £3,121,500, which is the highest threshold published; nothing is published about wealth above £10m. "Estimating aggregate household wealth can be difficult as the wealthiest households can be underrepresented." Accreditation of the survey was suspended from this round in June 2025.

sources.title: Inheritance Tax liabilities statistics
sources.edition: Estates passing on death in 2023 to 2024
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. Table 12.1a: 220 taxpaying estates above £10m in 2023-24 paid £1,040m of inheritance tax, 15% of the total, at an average effective rate of 18%, lower than the 25% paid by estates between £3m and £7.5m.

sources.title: Universal Credit quarterly statistics, 29 April 2013 to 14 May 2026
sources.notes: 8.4 million people on Universal Credit in May 2026. By immigration status, 84.5% are in the Common Travel Area group (UK, Ireland or right of abode); with the EU Settlement Scheme and indefinite leave to remain the three account for 96.2%, "in line with the general principle that only people who are settled in the UK or protected by the EU Exit Withdrawal Agreement should be able to claim Universal Credit".

sources.title: Public funds
sources.notes: "The NRPF condition means you will not be able to claim most benefits, tax credits or housing assistance that are paid by the state." Contributory benefits, including the state pension, are not public funds and can be claimed by people with no recourse to public funds who have the contribution record.

sources.title: UK to deliver on 5% NATO pledge as Government drives greater security for working people
sources.notes: "With the new 5% commitment on national security, the UK expects a projected split of 3.5% (core defence) and 1.5% (resilience and security) to be agreed at the NATO summit, with a target date of 2035."

sources.title: Statistics on International Development: provisional UK official development assistance spend 2025
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. UK aid was £13,036m in 2025, 0.43% of gross national income, down from 0.50% in 2024. The UK spent 0.7% of national income on aid from 2013 to 2020. 18.3% of aid in 2025 was spent inside the UK on refugee and asylum costs.

sources.title: Independent Water Commission: final report
sources.notes: The Cunliffe review. Water companies will spend £104bn on investment and operation over the five years to 2030, about £44bn of it enhancement. Footnote 569 gives the sector capital value as £103bn in 2024-25. Paragraph 684 records that the review was barred by its terms of reference from considering public ownership.

sources.title: Financial Stability Report
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Quoted: moves in gilt yields were "amplified by hedge fund deleveraging" during the most volatile period after the onset of the Middle East conflict; global sovereign issuance at historically high levels with higher proportions at shorter maturities; "any negative change in expectations could have wider consequences for sovereign debt markets". Bank of England material; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Bank Insights: What were the drivers of UK long-term interest rates in 2025?
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Quoted: "the primary driver of the increases in long rates was higher term premia"; rises "can largely be attributed to global factors, such as geopolitical uncertainty and concerns around fiscal sustainability"; 30-year yields at their highest since the turn of the century. Bank of England material; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: The policy landscape 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Quoted: "As John Healey puts together his first Budget, the backdrop of bond market turmoil limits the room for manoeuvre"; "£1 in every £12 of public spending now goes on debt interest"; "With energy bills rising again this winter, the cost-of-living crisis is back centre stage". Resolution Foundation; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Chancellor letter to the Treasury Select Committee: Budget 2026 date
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. The Chancellor commissioned the OBR to "prepare an economic and fiscal forecast for publication on 28 October 2026. This will be accompanied by the Budget." Also: "Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security. That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East."
